title: Valuing a firm, with and without profit growth
summary: Firm value as the present value of current and future profits, constant profits forever, the two growth formulas and their worked examples.

chunks.heading: Firm value and profit maximization
chunks.explanation_md:
**The value of a firm equals the present value of current and future profits (cash flows):**

**PV(firm) = π₀ + π₁/(1 + i)^1 + π₂/(1 + i)^2 + π₃/(1 + i)^3 + ...**

Here π (pi) stands for profit: π₀ is this period's profit, π₁ next period's, and so on. This period's profit is not discounted.

A **common assumption among economists** is that the **firm's goal is to maximize profits**. The slide explains what that really means: maximizing **the present value of current and future profits**, so **the firm is maximizing its value**.

key_terms.meaning: The present value of current and future profits (cash flows).

chunks.exam_line: PV(firm) = π₀ + π₁/(1 + i) + π₂/(1 + i)^2 + ...; maximizing profits means maximizing the PV of current and future profits, i.e. the firm's value.

chunks.heading: Constant profits forever: the $50,000 firm
chunks.explanation_md:
**Question:** a firm earns **constant annual profits of $50,000**, all paid out as dividends, **forever**. Current profits **have yet to be paid out**, and the interest rate is **10%**. What is the firm worth?

**How the slide reads it:**
- The dividend never changes: it stays at **$50,000 indefinitely**.
- The $50,000 **hasn't been paid to the owner yet**; it will be paid at the **end of this year**. So **no current payment exists**: π₀ = 0.

**Given:** π₀ = 0; π = $50,000; i = 10%.

**Working:** PV(firm) = π₀ + π / i = 0 + 50,000 / 0.10 = **$500,000**

The π / i part is just the perpetuity formula CF / i, with profit as the cash flow.
chunks.exam_line: Constant $50,000 profits forever, first paid at the end of this year, at 10%: PV(firm) = 0 + 50,000 / 0.10 = $500,000.

chunks.heading: Profits that grow: two formulas
chunks.explanation_md:
Now suppose **profits grow at a constant rate g**, and **current period profits are π₀**. The slide gives two formulas, and the only difference is the timing of this period's dividend:

- **Before current profits have been paid out as dividends:**
  **PV(firm) = π₀ × (1 + i) / (i - g)**
- **Immediately after current profits are paid out as dividends:**
  **PV(firm) = π₀ × (1 + g) / (i - g)**

Memory trick: **before** payout the top is **(1 + i)**; **after** payout the top is **(1 + g)**. The bottom is always **(i - g)**.

key_terms.meaning: The constant rate at which the firm's profits grow each period.

chunks.exam_line: Before payout: PV(firm) = π₀(1 + i)/(i - g). Immediately after payout: PV(firm) = π₀(1 + g)/(i - g).

chunks.heading: Worked example: $20,000 profits growing at 3%
chunks.explanation_md:
**Question:** current profits are **$20,000**, expected to **grow at 3% a year forever**. Dividends equal profits and the interest rate is **10%**. What is the firm worth now, and immediately after it pays this year's dividend?

**Given:** π = 20,000; g = 3%; i = 10%.

**Case 1: value of the firm (before the dividend is paid)**

PV(firm) = π₀ × (1 + i)/(i - g) = 20,000 × (1 + 0.10)/(0.10 - 0.03) = **$314,285.71**

**Case 2: value immediately after it pays a dividend equal to profits**

PV(firm) = π₀ × (1 + g)/(i - g) = 20,000 × (1 + 0.03)/(0.10 - 0.03) = **$294,285.71**

Check: the two answers differ by exactly $20,000, the dividend that was just paid out.
chunks.exam_line: $20,000 growing at 3%, i = 10%: before payout $314,285.71; immediately after payout $294,285.71.

chunks.heading: Practice: a software firm under four growth scenarios
chunks.explanation_md:
**Practice question:** a software company's CFO wants a valuation assuming the firm stays a single entity forever. **Current profits are $3.2 billion (not yet paid to shareholders)** and the interest rate is **9 percent**. Value the firm if profits **grow at 11%**, **grow at 4%**, **grow at 0%**, or **decline at 4%** a year.

Here is the working. Profits are **not yet paid**, so use the **before-payout** formula: PV(firm) = π₀ × (1 + i)/(i - g), with π₀ = 3.2 billion and i = 0.09. The top is 3.2 × 1.09 = 3.488 every time.

1. **g = 11%:** i - g = 0.09 - 0.11 = -0.02. The bottom is negative, so the formula gives -174.4 billion, a negative value for a firm earning positive profits.
2. **g = 4%:** 3.488 / (0.09 - 0.04) = 3.488 / 0.05 = **$69.76 billion**
3. **g = 0%:** 3.488 / 0.09 ≈ **$38.76 billion**
4. **g = -4% (decline):** 3.488 / (0.09 + 0.04) = 3.488 / 0.13 ≈ **$26.83 billion**

Pattern: the faster profits grow, the higher the firm's value.
chunks.exam_line: Not yet paid means use π₀(1 + i)/(i - g); higher growth gives a higher value.

questions.stem: The CFO of a software company wants a valuation assuming the firm remains a single entity forever. Current profits are $3.2 billion (not yet paid to shareholders) and the interest rate is 9 percent. Value the firm if profits (i) grow at 11%, (ii) grow at 4%, (iii) grow at 0%, (iv) decline at 4% a year. Comment on the results.
questions.model_answer_md:
This is a growing-firm valuation, so the first job is to pick the right formula.

**Choosing the formula.** Profits are **not yet paid**, so use the **before-payout** formula:

**PV(firm) = π₀ x (1 + i)/(i - g)**

**Given:** π₀ = $3.2 billion; i = 9% = 0.09. The top is the same every time: 3.2 x 1.09 = **3.488**.

**Working ($ billion):**

| Scenario | g | i - g | PV(firm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) Grow at 11% | 0.11 | 0.09 - 0.11 = -0.02 | 3.488 / -0.02 = -174.4 |
| (ii) Grow at 4% | 0.04 | 0.09 - 0.04 = 0.05 | 3.488 / 0.05 = **69.76** |
| (iii) Grow at 0% | 0 | 0.09 | 3.488 / 0.09 ≈ **38.76** |
| (iv) Decline at 4% | -0.04 | 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.13 | 3.488 / 0.13 ≈ **26.83** |

**Comment:**
- **Scenario (i):** when g is above i, the bottom (i - g) turns negative and the formula gives a negative value for a firm earning positive profits. That answer makes no sense, so the formula cannot be used when profits grow faster than the interest rate.
- **Scenarios (ii) to (iv):** the faster profits grow, the higher the value: $69.76 billion at 4%, about $38.76 billion with no growth and about $26.83 billion when profits shrink.
- With **zero growth** the formula becomes π₀(1 + i)/i, close to the perpetuity idea of profit divided by the interest rate.

**Conclusion:** use the before-payout formula because profits are not yet paid; firm value rises with the growth rate, and the formula only works while the growth rate stays below the interest rate.

rubric.point: Profits not yet paid, so use PV(firm) = π₀(1 + i)/(i - g)

g = 11%: i - g negative, formula gives a meaningless negative value
g = 4%: $69.76 billion
g = 0%: about $38.76 billion; g = -4%: about $26.83 billion
Higher growth gives a higher firm value

questions.stem: Explain firm valuation as covered in the session: the present value of a firm, its link to profit maximization, and the formulas for constant and growing profits. Use the session's examples.
questions.model_answer_md:
A firm is worth what its profits are worth today. The session builds this up in three steps.

**1. Value of a firm.** The value of a firm equals the **present value of current and future profits (cash flows)**:

**PV(firm) = π₀ + π₁/(1 + i)^1 + π₂/(1 + i)^2 + π₃/(1 + i)^3 + ...**

**2. Link to profit maximization.** A **common assumption among economists** is that the firm's goal is to **maximize profits**. This means maximizing **the present value of current and future profits**, so **the firm is maximizing its value**.

**3. Constant profits forever.**
- Example: constant annual profits of **$50,000**, all paid as dividends, **forever**; current profits **not yet paid**; i = **10%**.
- The first $50,000 is paid at the **end of this year**, so **π₀ = 0**.
- PV(firm) = π₀ + π / i = 0 + 50,000 / 0.10 = **$500,000** (the perpetuity formula with profit as the cash flow).

**4. Profits growing at a constant rate g.**
- **Before current profits are paid out:** **PV(firm) = π₀(1 + i)/(i - g)**
- **Immediately after they are paid out:** **PV(firm) = π₀(1 + g)/(i - g)**
- Example: current profits **$20,000**, growing at **3%** forever, i = **10%**:
  - Before payout: 20,000 x (1 + 0.10)/(0.10 - 0.03) = **$314,285.71**
  - After payout: 20,000 x (1 + 0.03)/(0.10 - 0.03) = **$294,285.71**
  - The gap is exactly the $20,000 dividend paid out.

**Conclusion:** a firm's value is the PV of its profits; maximizing profits means maximizing that value, and the right formula depends on whether profits are constant or growing and on whether this period's dividend has been paid.

questions.stem: Explain how the value of a firm is linked to the goal of profit maximization.
questions.model_answer_md:
The session connects what a firm is worth to what it aims for.

- **Value of a firm:** the **present value of current and future profits (cash flows)**:
  **PV(firm) = π₀ + π₁/(1 + i)^1 + π₂/(1 + i)^2 + π₃/(1 + i)^3 + ...**
- Here π₀ is this period's profit, which is not discounted; later profits are discounted like any future amount.
- **Profit maximization:** a **common assumption among economists** is that the **firm's goal is to maximize profits**. This means maximizing **the present value of current and future profits**.
- So **the firm is maximizing its value**.

In short, maximizing profits over time and maximizing firm value are the same goal.

questions.stem: A firm earns constant annual profits of $50,000, all paid as dividends, forever. Current profits have yet to be paid out and the interest rate is 10%. Calculate the value of the firm.
questions.model_answer_md:
Constant profits forever form a perpetuity, so we use the perpetuity idea.

**Reading the question:** the dividend never changes and stays at **$50,000 indefinitely**. It has not been paid yet; it will be paid at the **end of this year**, so **no current payment exists: π₀ = 0**.

**Formula:** PV(firm) = π₀ + π / i

**Given:** π₀ = 0; π = $50,000; i = 10% = 0.10.

**Working:** PV(firm) = 0 + 50,000 / 0.10 = **$500,000**

**Comment:** π / i is the perpetuity formula CF / i with profit as the cash flow.

PV(firm) = π₀ + π / i
Link to the perpetuity formula CF / i

questions.stem: Differentiate between the value of a growing firm before and immediately after current profits are paid out. Illustrate with current profits of $20,000 growing at 3% forever and an interest rate of 10%.
questions.model_answer_md:
The two values differ only in whether this period's dividend is still inside the firm.

| Basis | Before payout | Immediately after payout |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | **PV(firm) = π₀(1 + i)/(i - g)** | **PV(firm) = π₀(1 + g)/(i - g)** |
| Top | (1 + i) | (1 + g) |
| Working | 20,000 x 1.10 / 0.07 = 22,000 / 0.07 | 20,000 x 1.03 / 0.07 = 20,600 / 0.07 |
| Value | **$314,285.71** | **$294,285.71** |

**Given:** π = 20,000; g = 3%; i = 10%; i - g = 0.10 - 0.03 = 0.07.

**Comment:** the two values differ by exactly **$20,000**, the dividend just paid out. Use the before formula when profits are not yet paid, and the after formula once they have been.

After payout: π₀(1 + g)/(i - g)

Difference equals the $20,000 dividend paid
